items.title: Why Were Victorian Elites so Effective? (Works in Progress Magazine, Sam Hughes)
items.text:
## Amazing (long) read, highly recommend

I like Works in Progress. *A lot*. It's a serious outlet for long-form journalism, and it (usually!) features writers whose minds are oriented correctly toward the future. (its editor-in-chief lost his mind during 'rona, so I've stayed away from reading/subscribing or even attempting to contribute... *but I'm often very tempted*)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160670)

## What's the Key For Success?

Work hard, long hours, education, 5am, cold plunges, diversity, pay your politicians well to avoid corruption *blah-blah*?

No, no:

> The elites of Victorian Britain operated differently. Their schools and universities were not terribly academic and had very little STEM. As adults, **they got up late, drank a lot, and spent a remarkable share of their waking hours partying.** They loved feasting, sports, holidays, dancing, and dressing up. Contrary to their stodgy reputation, they were probably a lot of fun.

> the elites of nineteenth-century Britain were, by their own lights, extremely successful. For much of the century, Britain was the richest country on Earth. Its companies dominated global commerce, industry and finance.

## In Defence of Debauchery

![](https://m.stacker.news/160674)

* **SCHOOLING:** while strict (early age, regulated times, single-sex away from family, corporal punishment), the values the English Victorian elite cultivated at boarding school were remarkably progressive: loyalty, internationalism, studies of the arts -- Latin and Ancient Greek --

Amazing:

> There was **resistance to the teaching of science, not because Victorians were hostile to science** in principle, but because they thought it **irrelevant to the kind of moral and cultural formation** that a school for gentlemen was supposed to provide.
> (By contrast, girls were not usually taught classics, meaning that, rather surprisingly, affluent Victorian girls generally followed a more modern curriculum than their brothers.)

While not obviously successful, it cultivated valuable skills:

> ...The most that can be said for Victorians’ classical education is perhaps that, like schooling in any difficult subject, it trained students in self-discipline, memorization, and applying rules.

And *this* we could definitely learn from today:

> Under such circumstances, it is perhaps unsurprising that the share of time spent in the classroom was relatively modest. At Rugby School, weeks were divided into three ‘full days’, three ‘half days’, and Sunday. On a full day, students spent about five hours in the classroom, compared with maybe two hours on a half day.  \[AND, importantly:] They also tended to be shorter than those of contemporary elite schools in France, Germany, or Italy, where the curriculum was normally more academically rigorous.

## "Victorians thought extremely highly of sports, believing that they instilled team spirit and endurance, fostered mutual loyalty, channeled energy and competitiveness, and taught men how to win and lose graciously."

One Loretto School headmaster described the school's priorities: **1) character, 2) physique,** 3) intelligence, 4) manners, 5) information. First time *brawns > brains, eh*

* **UNIVERSITIES**: Not much studying, plenty of "teambuilding"

I found *this* observation interesting:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160677)

> Oxbridge tutors believed overwhelmingly that the purpose of an undergraduate degree was not training for work nor even preparation for academic research, but rather a general moral and intellectual formation that would fit students for any professional role they might later pursue.

also:

> Fellowships were opened up to laymen in the later decades of the century, but **Oxford and Cambridge did not become world-leading research institutions until they were transformed by German scholars fleeing Nazism in the 1930s.** The dominance of Oxbridge in British culture was unusual: these institutions educated a much larger share of the elite than was the case for any two institutions in any other country

Fuck, these peeps just had *great* lives. (In some respects, Oxford life these days is very similar!)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160679)

* **ADULTHOOD**: Busy-busy-fucking busy bee... but not in the way you think

## "One virtue that upper-class Victorian education signally failed to inculcate was early rising. Although Victorian schoolboys and university students got up fairly early for chapel, the day of an upper-class Victorian adult started late."

Fuck *yeah!* Den loves victory https://stacker.news/items/1590741

The great statesmen and prime ministers back then "breakfasted at 9 am" or hosted a "social breakfast starting at 10.30 am (claret was served), continuing till about noon." **A-M-A-Z-I-N-G**

Also, not that different from today (minus the frock)

> general, however, Britain’s elites were slow to suburbanize, and in 1914 most still lived in centrally located row houses and walked to work. Every day a great herd of frock-coated men emerged from Belgravia and Mayfair and poured through Covent Garden to their offices in Parliament, Whitehall, the Inns of Court, and the City.

If you've noticed the drinking *at every goddamn meal*, you're not alone. It's pretty disturbing, an entire nation run by high-functioning alcoholics.

> The Victorians loved drinking and drank a lot by modern standards. Men drank more than women, but women drank a good deal too: one conduct guide[noted that](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/12426/pg12426-images.html)‘young ladies seldom drink more than three glasses of wine at dinner but married ladies, professional ladies, and those accustomed to society, and habits of affluence, will habitually take five or even six, whether in their own homes or at the tables of their friends’.

...and the partying, until the wee hours. Plus, for some odd reason Americans call this "Irish exit" (or French goodbye):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160682)

And they were hardly just for entertainment:

> the social events of the Victorian elite were notable for their lack of segregation by age or sex. A Society ball discharged the functions of both a teenage house party and a business networking convention: in fact, it*was* both a teenage house party and a business networking convention. \[...] Unmarried young people (and their unfortunate parents) might go to three or four balls per week, while other Society members would go to one or two. But the other nights were scarcely less busy. Opera, theatre and concerts were important, especially opening or gala nights.

Fuck, dudes kept busy.

> An MP might miss dinner for a late sitting of Parliament, but still drop into a soirée at 10.30pm, turn up to a supper party at 11.45pm, and then arrive at a ball at 1am. From February to July, the Victorian upper class led a remarkably nocturnal existence, with bedtimes in the small hours and the mornings something of a write-off.

## "All else being equal, rich and powerful Victorians must have been less productive for spending four hours a day in the office rather than twelve. But the creation of a single ruling *Gemeinschaft* may have had compensatory advantages."

Domestic and international (geo)political implications:

> This obviously had advantages for Britain. The elites of the American South had a very different identity to those of the North, and ultimately led the country into civil war. Spain, Italy and France suffered from incessant conflicts between urban bourgeois and rural nobility. Germany was riven with strife along geographical, religious, and class lines. **Some of these tensions existed in Britain, but except in Ireland, the elite finessed them peacefully.**

## "Would modern societies work better if their local and national government were conducted by a tight-knit community of extremely rich and successful people?"

The author thinks not... but a kid can dream, longing as we do for the best moment in (modern) Western civilization: the Victorian era.

items.title: How to Get People to Use Bitcoin
items.text:
For many years, I’ve been trying to figure out how to get bitcoin into people’s hands. Even long-time bitcoiners often don’t want to pay with bitcoin. At best, they slowly accumulate it, and they don’t really feel like they’re missing anything. They buy it on exchanges, pay fees, expose their personal information, and need a third party’s blessing for every transaction.

I sometimes hear people say that bitcoin doesn’t need anyone and that, on the contrary, we need bitcoin. I see it a little differently. To me, bitcoin is something like a living organism. I consider its creation to be an event almost as rare as the emergence of life itself. But for bitcoin to truly live and serve us as better money, I believe it needs users.

With every transaction, a new connection is created or an existing one is strengthened. Users gradually get better at securing their bitcoin, demand better tools, and bitcoin becomes more resilient.

That’s why I don’t think adoption is some kind of optional bonus.
**Adoption is a fundamental condition for bitcoin to actually be useful.**

## I tried various approaches

* I liked the idea of bringing bitcoin directly into Signal, for example: https://stacker.news/items/85702
  * But Signal still hasn’t added bitcoin support, and I’m afraid there simply isn’t enough incentive for them to do so anytime soon.
* Years ago, I also created an app that allowed people to load bitcoin onto an NFC card and pass it around much like cash: https://stacker.news/items/117623
  * Technically, it worked. But there wasn’t enough interest. It was a nice project, but it didn’t solve a real problem for people.
* Later, I also looked into why even bitcoiners themselves often don’t want to pay with bitcoin: https://stacker.news/items/210830

## It’s not enough to let merchants accept bitcoin

In the meantime, I onboarded dozens of businesses and bitcoiners locally.

Most of them were just isolated points on a map. A business started accepting bitcoin, but nobody actually paid with it. Eventually, the merchant forgot how to accept a bitcoin payment or what to do with the bitcoin they received.

It wasn’t until about a year ago that I managed to partially break through this problem.

I onboarded another business simply because we went there regularly. And to this day, every week we come there in a changing group of people, with everyone paying in bitcoin. https://stacker.news/items/1584550

![](https://m.stacker.news/159586)

The pub owner didn’t want bitcoin at all in the beginning. What matters to him is us as customers who come to his pub because of bitcoin. In the end, a merchant will accept pretty much any form of payment. What’s more important is finding people who are willing to pay with bitcoin.

Here, we use bitcoin also as a filter for finding interesting people. Anyone willing to pay with bitcoin is kind of open-minded, and it’s a pleasure to get to know them over a regular lunch.

## I don’t want to depend on a single app again

Over the years, I’ve recommended various wallets and tools to people. Some of them eventually disappeared.

The custodial version of Wallet of Satoshi, which was the most popular one, stopped working. Alza, the largest retailer in the Czech Republic and one of the first major merchants to accept bitcoin, started requiring additional administrative steps when paying with bitcoin. Qerko, which allowed bitcoin payments at around 1,000 businesses, removed bitcoin support.

At first, this was pretty discouraging. It was the end of 2025, and at the same time the price of bitcoin dropped significantly. I had to figure out what to do with the dozens of people I had introduced to a particular app, which was now no longer going to work for them.

I felt a little trapped. With every app, there was a risk that I would have to repeat the whole migration process again at any time.

But in January 2026, it also seemed to me that AI models had improved significantly, so I decided to try building my own wallet. One that I had been carrying around in my head for years.

## Linky

Linky is a bitcoin wallet and, at the same time, a communication layer for the people you want to use bitcoin with.

You can add your contacts, send them messages and bitcoin. You can pay any Lightning invoice. You can load bitcoin in the form of Cashu tokens onto an NFC card or send it to someone in a message — even to someone who doesn’t use Linky at all.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159587)

But I’m also trying to build a certain degree of antifragility into it.

From the beginning, I’ve been building Linky so that the app doesn’t depend on a particular operator. There are already other instances running on different domains. If my instance stopped working tomorrow, the network wouldn’t necessarily have to disappear with it.

We achieve this through a combination of three decentralized technologies:

* **Cashu** for bitcoin,
* **Nostr** for communication,
* **Evolu** for data storage.

We use several other interesting technologies as well, but I don’t want to get into the technical details here. There are now six other developers working on Linky. One of them is a close friend of mine who has been improving the app very intensively, primarily on the technical side.

What started as a funny vibecoded app is gradually becoming a serious project.

Around 250 people are currently testing Linky in the local group, and several hundred more users are using it.

## Individuals

People use Linky because they like it.

Thanks to its simplicity and steadily increasing reliability, it is gradually becoming the primary bitcoin wallet for many people.

**However, most people still don’t actually need a lightning wallet.** 😢

You can build a great wallet. You can onboard merchants. You can explain the benefits of bitcoin to people.
But if they have no reason to use bitcoin, all of those things will remain just flashes of activity.

## Proxy Payments

Recently, however, we managed to create a feature that I think can at least partially solve this problem. We call it **proxy payments**.

In the Czech Republic, people increasingly use QR codes for bank transfers. You can find them in online shops as well as physical stores.

For users, this is still somewhat less convenient than paying by card, but merchants love it because they don’t have to pay card-network fees.

Today, I can pay with bitcoin at any of these businesses. No fees and no KYC.

I scan the payment QR code using Linky - just as if I were paying a lightning invoice. Linky offers me the option to send the payment request to my contacts.

I select several friends and send them the offer.

Whoever accepts it first receives the payment details from the QR code. They pay the merchant from their bank account, and I send them sats in return.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159589)

## Does it worth the effort?

Maybe this sounds like a pointless detour. Why would I ask someone else to pay by bank transfer on my behalf when I could simply pay myself?

For me, it’s useful because I don’t have to hold fiat that is losing value.

For my friends, it’s useful because they don’t have to use an exchange, pay fees, or expose their personal information. They acquire bitcoin in an interactive way — usually in small amounts.

As a side benefit for everyone, there is the more abstract fact that you are building the bitcoin network and thereby helping ensure that you’ll be able to use bitcoin in the future as well.

To use proxy payments comfortably, you need roughly two or three people. Most payments are completed within two minutes. It’s not as direct or fast as paying by card, but it works surprisingly well.

Linky is showing people new ways to use bitcoin.

**Come help us test and build our shared bitcoin network. 🙏**

items.title: Bank Runs are Good, Actually: Death to the Central Banks (FT, Toby Nangle)
items.text:
ASTONISHING piece to see in regular financial press. *Maybe the tide is turning and the world is healing?*

![](https://m.stacker.news/159395)

The basic/most fundamental rationale for a central bank isn't financing the gov deficit (which they don't...*ish*) or set centralized interest rates, but to support commercial banks when faced with bank runs (=stand ready to lend against their assets, even if distressed, with newly created base money, so stave off the run.) The idea, from Francis Barings to Diamond\&Dybvig's [Nobel Prize](https://stacker.news/items/1583458?commentId=1583534) winning article, is that depositors are fickle and might/will run on perfectly healthy banks *and* that such runs cause real damage to the economy (*and* might spread through the banking system like wildfire and we all collapse into Great Depression 2.0).
*That's everything that's wrong with monetary economics and politics around central banks in one sentence...*

***

The authors of the paper Nangle discusses here used the Chronicling America project, scanned newspapers, then...

> they used LLMs to sift these articles further to find pieces about actual bank runs rather than, say, stuff about boats running into river banks, or the local bank manager running for mayor, and to match each report to individual banks.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159396)

> According to Verner, the research reveals that the idea that runs kill solvent banks is dramatically overstated. It turns out that depositors are actually pretty good at working out how dodgy a bank is, generally making runs on banks that are insolvent or very close to insolvent.

This is incredible. Specifically, — and I'm sparing you a deep dive into debates in financial history and monetary economics here — a big rationale for *why central banks must exist* is **to prevent bad types of bank runs.**

Running a bank means it has to shed assets, assets that aren't "finished," or turned into workable projects and thus liqudity, yet. (That's sort of the purpuse of a bank: to *liquify* illiquid assets, hold the maturity and duration mismatch in the meantime.)  Selling these assets quickly means taking (large) haircuts on book value, meaning a random run on a healthy bank can destroy projects or at least turn the bank itself bankrupt -- destroying customer relatioships and disrupting the bank-money-level money supply etc etc. 
**That's all unnecessary, and a benevolent central bank/observer can improve upon the state of the world by injecting more money and support the healthy bank.**

## ...except, depositors don't run on healthy banks!

That's what this beautiful history and database shows. Somehow, depositors (in aggregate) are clever enough to sniff out when something is wrong *and not* structurally/mindlessly/sunspot-style make erratic and concentrated mistakes.

If you scratch [the lender or last resort literature a little](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/when-did-the-bank-of-england-become-a-lender-of-last-resort/), you find that it's a good, disciplining market mechanism for depositors to run on banks. Here's a schematic:

* if bank is healthy and other bankers know it, then the bank can source enough liquidity from them ("recycling" deposits), against a very minimal short-term expense. **No problem, no negative outcome, no need for lender of last resort** 
* if the bank is unhealthy and the other bankers know it, they won't lend to it and it will fail, *and it will be a good thing!* Bankers taking bad risks or making bad investments should fail, like every other business in a market economy.
* if the bank is healthy, but the **other bankers don't know it** *and so refuse to lend*, that's when a lender of last resort needs to step in and save the day. By supplying that extra liquidity it can stave off the damaging run and everyone is better off for it.

Here's the best short article/overview I've ever seen on this (by [George Kaufman, for econlib](https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/BankRuns.html)):

![](https://m.stacker.news/159394)

---

The literature on bank runs and central banks is basically an exercise in showing **whether or not the central bank knows about the true state of a given bank better than other bankers do.**

When central banks *also* had prudential obligation, by chance some of its workers would have recently audited and inspected private information for that bank, meaning it's quite plausible that central bankers *do* have some insider information here that they can act on. (Nowadays that function is usually separated to another agency, thus the argument is practically quite moot.)

But... If historically and practically depositors are good enough in aggregate to sniff out what's wrong, there's no *need* for a central bank to intervene and override their market choice.

Bank runs are bad for local economies

> ...only if the banks that are being abandoned have been making bad loans, a big borrower defaults, or something like that.

...in which case there is **a real economic loss that we want/need someone to carry** — not paper over and pretend it's not there. (\_cough\_, Bitfinex...)

***

Told yah:

> Surely **the mere process of a run on a healthy bank wreaked havoc on their local economy?** Apparently not.

> Cross-referencing each bank’s financial strength, the researchers trace the local economic impact of each bank run using Bradstreet’s contemporary reporting. They find that a run on a strong bank doesn’t really impose any economic cost at all on the local economy. Yet runs on banks whose fundamentals are awful are followed by major lending contractions that can cause all sorts of spillover problems.

and:

> Out of **3,984 bank runs on individual US banks from 1863–1934**, the authors identify 53 that look like they’re based on “misinformation” or “depositor confusion”, which reads as academese for “blind panic”. Of these 53 oddities, six banks failed, which sounds like maybe six too many. But the researchers argue that the historical data indicates that “strong banks (fundamentals in the upper tercile) subject to **non-fundamental runs have a zero probability of failure”**
> one of the footnotes indicates that at least one of these failed banks had basically committed massive fraud, which was only uncovered by their so-called irrational run.

*Even that*, the depositors sniffed out. Amazing.

***

All "pretty interesting" says Nangle, understating the explosive result.

> the ideas that the Nobel winners formalise are really the ones sitting behind the rationale for bank deposit insurance.

Yes. This evidence shows/weighs heavy that lender of last resort is a defunct and unnecessary function — liable to abuse, nepotism, and trigger-happy rulers, not actually saving a banking system that needs it

## Runs are good. Banks should fail more. And lender of last resort is an unnecessary function

items.title: Book Review: Broken Money and the Way Out, PART 1: MONEY (the Invity Team)
items.text:
TAKEAWAY NUMERO UNO: If there's a successful book titled *Broken Money*, you DO NOT title your own marketing pamphlet/e-book style "Broken Money" as well.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159635)

***

I spent some time today looking through the Invity people's fintech offering. We met at BTCHEL, where they launched/announced some cool banking features for us Europooreans. https://stacker.news/items/1580878, https://stacker.news/items/1581849 https://stacker.news/items/1585380

Particularly, quite convenient **auto-stacking, payment cards with bitcoin/stablecoins,** and **juicy-af cashback** on every spend. (Up to stupidly [low maximums](https://www.invity.io/personal-accounts), it turns out -.-)

This is all very tempting, and Den is a sucker for a good sats deal (*aren't we all?!*), so what does a bookish nerd do?

## Download and read the free e-book, of course!

***

It's from their educational platform, Invity Academy (as if we didn't have enough educational outlets...):

> It is meant for people who know Bitcoin from headlines and debates, but never got an answer to the most important question: why did it come about at all, and what problem does it solve?
> We start with money itself — how it came about, how it works today, and why so many people feel that something about it „broke“. Only once we understand the problem does it make sense to talk about a solution.

Oh, turns out this is *really* for Mr. Den. Let's dig in.

*Blah-blah-blah*, money's three functions, and various properties (ignoring, for now, Erik Yakes' *7th Property*, **Immutability** https://stacker.news/items/1572208)

![](https://m.stacker.news/159636)

...gold, commodity money, stock-to-flows. Alright, amazing. State intervention, Roman coins.

## "If you were born after 1971, you live in a historical anomaly"

Pretty neat account:

* 1870-1914: Classical gold standard
* 1933: gold banned
* 1971 Nixon Shock

They definitely overdo the importance of 1971, a mere formality in a world already addicted to fiat and money printing. (1914 is a more important civilizational cutoff.)

Cool, but graphs like these are pretty boring. A *dollar*, like *a* bitcoin, is not a meaningful economic unit; nobody (rationally) cares about *a* dollar, but the relationship between what they have and earn to what they invest and consume. e.g., https://stacker.news/items/737272, https://stacker.news/items/1578595

![](https://m.stacker.news/159637)

> 1913 the Fed, 1933 the ban on holding gold, 1944 Bretton Woods, 1971 the Nixon Shock — four steps from hard money to fiat. → Since 1971 no currency in the world has been backed by anything tangible

VERY nice

![](https://m.stacker.news/159638)

> How money is actually created today
> → The vast majority of the money in your account was created by commercial banks, not the state.
> → New money comes into being at the moment of a loan. When you repay the loan, the money disappears.
> → QE lets a central bank create money in the order of trillions within weeks.
> → The M2 money supply grows substantially faster than real output.

## AMAZINGLY witty: "Money-supply inflation is the cause, price inflation is the symptom."

![](https://m.stacker.news/159639)

Here's a scary graph, but of course *financing conditions* matters too: An average interest rate for mortgages in Czechia was about [7% in 2000](https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Average-mortgage-loan-interest-rate-1995-2005_fig7_24080862); [below 5%](https://www.globalpropertyguide.com/europe/czech-republic/mortgage-interest-rate) in 2025.

## Inflation as a silent tax

![](https://m.stacker.news/159641)

> Modern central banking is often defended with the argument that it stimulates the economy and creates jobs. Even if we take that at face value, we must at the same time see the flip side: the money a central bank creates does not arrive for everyone at once. It travels a predictable path that structurally favours one group over another.

VERY eloquent and punchy.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159640)

> At the end of the pipe stand

* **The fixed-wage employee**: the wage is usually adjusted only with a delay, and not by the full extent of inflation.
* **The pensioner** — the pension is indexed once a year, slowly.
* **The young family** without assets — they own no assets to rise in value, yet pay higher prices for food, energy, rent.
  -**The saver** on a savings account — the interest does not cover the loss of purchasing power

These things are conditional and not *obviously* and *always* the case; boomers in America enjoy pretty competitive COLAs; interest rates on savings accounts in Iceland are ~halfway between CPI and monetary expansion. With bond prices collapsing, rates on (high-yield, short-term) bank accounts like those at fintechs are bound to rise explosively. https://stacker.news/items/1578425

***

## NOTHING STOPS THIS LYN ALDEN TRAIN

Yeah, dudes didn't just *borrow* Lyn's title; they take her fiscal framework too: there's no way back/out from governments' profligacy and debt-to-GDP ratios. America just *cannot* outgrow [40trn in debt](https://stacker.news/items/1554591) (...unless we scalp the boomers https://stacker.news/items/1468968, you know the drill.)

> An economic term returning to the debate in recent years is fiscal dominance. It means a state of affairs where the state’s budgetary situation is so strained that the central bank cannot run an independent policy. Lyn Alden describes that the United States entered this situation around 2022. The interest cost on US federal debt exceeded the defence budget in 2024 — and that is a defence budget which is itself larger than the budgets of the next ten largest countries combined.

The financial FIXES that used to work:

* The **60/40 portfolio**: yeah, it's entirely dead. Also, bonds don't provide *neither* uncorrelated returns, nor inflation-adjusted returns at all.
* savings account: guaranteed losses. Czech republic example is \~4% interest on savings, 2.5% official inflation... BUT tax the nominal return 15% *and* assets like flats and properties rose *way more* than 1-2%.
* New fixes?

> Holding large cash in the bank is, over the long run, a strategy by which the state really taxes your purchasing power. Diversification remains valuable, but it must include assets that respond to monetary degradation (hard assets). Gold passed the test of 5,000 years. Neutral, apolitical, independent of the banking system. Bitcoin is new — it has 15 years behind it. But if its properties are confirmed, it offers everything gold does, and more: portability, verifiability, divisibility and neutrality in a form gold can never have.

...in PART 2, dudes move on to the orange solution: \_bitcoin\_, woop woop!

items.title: It's Ghey To Care About Climate Change (FT, Pilita Clark)
items.text:
Yeah, we all know the reason climate change ~~activism~~ delusion doesn't have a higher uptick is... *toxic masculinity*!

**oh lord.**

![](https://m.stacker.news/160711)

> **If you are a man who cares about climate change, are you a bit of a dweeb? Put another way, if a man says global warming is rubbish, does he seem more manly**? In my 15 years of writing about climate change, these are not questions I have considered before. But I have begun to do so since coming across research that suggests a lot of men brush off the climate problem for fear of seeming too feminine.

## why do studies and polls across the world consistently show that men care less about global warming than women?

It's all just socialization and sexism.

> Some studies suggest that men feel they have more to lose from policies to fight climate change. Others conclude it is because women are socialised to care more about things like the environment. items.title: Why Are Bond Yields Suddenly so High?! (FT, Chris Giles)
items.text:
*Great question, few good answers.*

![](https://m.stacker.news/160553)

"The big question is why yields have risen so much."

* Is it because investors want more compensation for perceived fiscal unsustainability?
* Does it reflect expectations of much faster growth?
* Is there a global war for investment funds and limited lenders?
* Has the Iran war raised the prospect of continued high inflation?
* Is it that central banks signalled the need for persistently higher short-term interest rates and markets are parroting this back?
* Have monetary policymakers lost inflation-fighting credibility?
* Or are bond markets now dominated by flighty hedge funds that can make huge returns if they get a negative narrative to stick?

Chris Giles goes through some of these and provide some decent rebuttals.

> Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said there were [three broad reasons](https://www.federalreserve.gov/mediacenter/files/FOMCpresconf20260916.pdf) at a press conference in September: US economic strength, competition for capital and difficult geopolitics.
> The more important thing he said, however, was that explanations for changes in bond yields “tend to be overdetermined”. In other words, there are many competing but unprovable theories. And he is right.

## "The single clearest cause of the rise in bond yields, as the chart below shows, was President Donald Trump’s decision to initiate war with Iran, before which yields were generally falling"

![](https://m.stacker.news/160554)

Seems obvious, but I'm still a little stuck on the **transmission mechanism** : there's no reason, in principle, that wars or even oil price shocks ought to result in higher yields

The analogy being the 1970 had a few other critical components: **labor unions aggressively striking** for higher wages, setting off a price-wage push; and **central banks eager to accommodate** the real-cost push with new money.

There's no risk for the former, as labor unions worldwide (minus the Nordics, but they're pretty meek here) are a ghost of their former self. And the latter is entirely under our own control; central bankers can decide not to accommodate oil price increases (or actively crush demand... ), thus gaining credibility for their monetary policy *and* an indication of how independent they are from the fiscal authorities.

I guess, then, the bond market is pragmatic and saying "Fat chance, Den; dream the fuck on — dudes will print."

STILL, I find it kind of weird, then, to jump past the intermediate steps and conclude that wars (or oil prices) cause inflation and thus yields.  **No, (central) *banks printing money* cause inflation, *always and everywhere*.** For immediate analogy: Planes don't crash because of gravity, even though of course gravity is involved and 'ultimately' the cause.

> There is no doubt that short-term interest rate expectations have risen across advanced economies. At the start of the year, the Fed was expected to cut rates to almost 3 per cent and now is expected to raise them to 4.75 per cent. That is a huge shift.

Another commonly quipped reason is that AI has unleashed *massive* productivity gains that are about to swamp GDP numbers -- thus rates ought to go up (via the real economy). So far, only a single quarter of a sliver of such indications. AND:

> anyone who remembers 2022, when the US Inflation Reduction Act led to excitement about green growth that did not materialise, should be wary of predicting a massive increase in US growth rates.

Also, this investment boom is not *that* visible (outside specific sectors):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160560)

The other option is that capital is *expensive* now, with AI debt issuance swallowing up all the air in the room, *lol mixing metaphors*:

> Higher yields could simply reflect a massive increase in demand for investible funds that is not met by increased supply. The chart below, which I have borrowed from Toby Nangle’s excellent piece, shows that debt issued by AI hyperscalers accounts for 13.8 per cent of US Treasury issuance, up from only 1.3 per cent in 2024. In other words, there has been a big increase in demand for debt from the AI sector.

> there could still be a general change in the balance between overall debt issuance and debt demand among investors. To the extent that the war for capital is a valid explanation of higher long-term yields, it is more a story of excess debt overall than one to be pinned on the tech bros.

## "No one I have spoken to thinks government debt markets in advanced economies are currently disorderly or signalling impending default."

eeeh, cute. *Maybe look further afield than your standard sources, fren*?!

***

Archive still messing w us... lmk if you want the full article -- lots of good graphs in there.

items.title: The long road to bitcoin payments...
items.text:
*Why bitcoin payments haven’t taken off, and a call for moonshot ideas that could change that*

“If \[bitcoin] ends up just being digital gold, I think it’s failed,” Jack Dorsey [said in January 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KyFkv5DGeUA&t=1250s). “If it ends up being a currency that people can use daily, then it’s succeeded.” Not everyone agrees. Many in bitcoin argue it must first succeed as a store of value, and that demand for payments will follow. So we start with a clear question: does the current path lead to irrelevance, or is it the expected grind of hardening bitcoin for the day it’s needed for payments? This report asks what is holding bitcoin payments back, and what moonshot ideas could speed up adoption.

Bitcoin payments work better than ever. Turning that progress into everyday use remains the challenge, and the time to move is now, as stablecoins are ready to gain rapid adoption.

**Where things stand.** Over the past seven years, bitcoin spending technology has improved dramatically. Lightning infrastructure runs in production, and self-custodial wallets now hide most of their complexity. Seven years ago, building a bitcoin payments app took more than a year and several developers. Today, anyone can build a working first version from a single prompt to an AI coding tool. Custodial bitcoin is now no harder to integrate than custodial stablecoins, though self-custodial bitcoin is still harder to run at scale. More than a million US merchants can accept bitcoin through Square. Yet few people pay with bitcoin in everyday life, a point most in the industry accept. The gap is mostly demand, not technology.

**Why now.** The wider financial system is being updated, raising an open question: will the rails chosen during this shift be hard to change later, or will payments follow what people want to pay and be paid in, with software making it easy to add any payment rail? As large payment providers update their rails, they are choosing stablecoins, not bitcoin. Stripe, Shopify and Coinbase are building stablecoins in, and major consumer products appear likely to follow. Stripe, Visa, American Express and Google have also joined a consortium launching a new stablecoin, OUSD, and the first protocol implementations for AI agent payments settle almost entirely in stablecoins. Developers build on the rails their tools support, and wallets ship with the networks their partners already use. AI agents are the clearest case. They need small, programmable payments, which Lightning suits, yet the first agent payment tools are being built around stablecoins and cards. If early choices do stick, bitcoin’s absence now could be hard to reverse. If they don’t, the question becomes demand alone.

**What’s blocking it?**

* **Demand:** neither side is pulling for it. Holders would rather save than spend, and bitcoin’s culture celebrates holding. Merchants prefer to receive and hold dollars, so few accept bitcoin, and new payment platforms leave it out.
* **Volatility and competition:** price swings make bitcoin hard to price goods in, and dollar stablecoins meet the need for stable payments.
* **Policy:** US tax treatment of every purchase and pending regulation.

**What could change this?** We’re looking for moonshot ideas: changes big enough to shift bitcoin payments, not just improve them. A few possible paths to start the discussion:

* **Shared rails:** let people pay in dollars or bitcoin over the same Lightning network, with a compelling reason to choose it, so bitcoin is one tap away wherever people already pay: in agent payments, merchant checkout and fintech apps.
* **Payments for people who need them most:** self-custodial bitcoin payments that better solve the needs of people facing capital controls or unstable currencies.
* **New reasons to spend:** spending incentives for existing holders.
* **New ways to spend:** product experiences that create entirely new kinds of payments, such as paying creators or AI services per use. The killer app for micropayments probably won’t feel like a traditional payment at all.

We don’t know which, if any, will work. That’s why we want to hear yours.

**What we’re asking.** Our central question: what moonshot ideas would create a believable, viable plan to accelerate bitcoin payments adoption? To make it explicit: what would it take for a major platform such as Meta, Shopify, or OpenAI to accept bitcoin? Builders: propose ideas and test them. Payment providers: share data on how people pay. Funders: back the most promising experiments and help foster demand. This is a living document. Read the [full report on GitHub](https://github.com/spiralxyz/bitcoin-payments), share your ideas or data in the replies below, or join the [GitHub discussion](https://github.com/spiralxyz/bitcoin-payments/discussions/1). We’ll keep updating the report as we learn.

items.title: Cognitive Mercantilism - Why you don't have to be a farmer - Venkatesh Rao
items.text:
This is an interesting article. Rao proposes the idea that the current AI-is-gonna-take-all-our-jobs panic that is seen in some quarters is a form of zero-sum, mercantilist thinking.

Referencing Joyce Appleby’s [*The Relentless Revolution: A History of Capitalism*](https://contraptions.venkateshrao.com/p/contraptions-book-club), Rao gives a nice summary of how Appleby (and I suppose Rao, too) characterize the mercantilist view:

![](https://m.stacker.news/163575)

This as opposed to a more positive-sum view of trade that might define capitalism (defining capitalism seems to be a difficult enough task for even the best of us: https://stacker.news/items/1416952/r/Scoresby)).

Rao suggests that we are making the same mistake as the mercantilists of yesteryear when we think about intelligence:

> Now replace *wealth* with *intelligence*, and *mercantilism* with *cognitive mercantilism*.
>
> The parallels are almost embarrassingly direct.
>
> First, intelligence is imagined as a fixed resource embodied in human brains and the knowledge products mined from them. The objective of national and corporate strategy becomes attracting the best brains, controlling their output, accumulating intellectual property, and maintaining a favorable balance of knowledge trade. The cognitive mercantilist wants to hoard intelligence and its products like bullion. The global competition for talent becomes a treasure hunt for genius brains and the valuable knowledge species they can produce, which now includes AIs in addition to copyrightable culture and patentable inventions.
>
> Second, supposedly stupid people cannot be trusted to think for themselves. They need to be governed by cognitive elites, who know better and must regulate the behavior of the less intelligent for their own good. Democratizing intelligence is dangerous because the masses will misuse it, fall for nonsense, or unleash chaos. The assumption is that intelligence is safe only in the hands of those already certified to possess it.
>
> Third, the supply of intelligence is treated as the central economic fact. Controlling its production, preserving its scarcity, and maintaining high prices for brains and knowledge products (including AIs) are the primary concerns. The demand side barely registers. Less intelligent people are regarded as limited cognitive laborers and passive consumers of whatever knowledge products elites choose to provide. They are not imagined as significant sources of demand for intelligence in their own right, let alone as participants in its further production.
>
> Fourth, the cognitive mercantilist assumes that most people are not good for much intellectually. If 80% of humanity is occupied in low-grade cognitive labor, or simply muddling along without producing much intelligence at all, that is unfortunate but natural. Automating their cognitive work merely threatens to create billions of useless minds to occupy.

There was a time when most of humanity was involved in producing food but technology has drastically reduced the number of people needed to feed us all:

> The agricultural revolution that helped launch capitalism began overturning the apparent necessity of having most of humanity engaged in farming. Over the following centuries, improvements in agricultural productivity reduced the fraction of the population required to produce food from a large majority to a tiny minority in advanced economies.
>
> The result was not a world full of useless mouths. It was a world in which vastly more people could do things other than farm, while enjoying access to vastly more food.

We seem, though, to have found uses for all the food we can produce...and then some. And so the same might be true for whatever the product of LLMs is:

# "The crucial economic question then becomes not how much intelligence people can produce, but *how much intelligence they can find uses for*."

![](https://m.stacker.news/163584)

> what if that demand is as elastic, inventive, and historically transformative as the demand for material goods turned out to be? What if the apparent surplus of human minds is an artifact of our inability to imagine what people might want to do in an intelligence-rich world?

Rao's argument begins to sound a little like the somewhat cliche: "it's gonna free us up from drudgery to do all sorts of wonderful things!"

> Abundant AI changes that calculation. Someone who previously had little reason to think hard about a problem may suddenly discover that a modest investment of attention unlocks enormous possibilities. They can build something, investigate something, understand something, or pursue an ambition that was previously out of reach.

But if I have to choose between the vision of AI taking everyone's jobs and killing us all, and the vision of AI inducing a huge wave of demand for new things that humans might do, I think the latter is more likely.

items.title: OpenBitcoin.com: A new bitcoin block explorer with guides tools and games
items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

items.title: Austin trip day one: Bitcoin all around
items.text:
Evening stackers,

I write from my hotel having just checked in and showered after a very long productive day.

I landed in Austin at 1045 AM and I had rented a Turo. It took me a frustratingly long time to find the damn thing but once I was was in the right garage (blue  not red) I found it pretty quickly. Then I went to my hotel, a grungy little thing 15 min south of round rock, only to be told I couldn’t check in for another 1.5 hours. I was looking forward to a shower and a nap before heading out to meet @Scoresby at PlebLab. No matter, the poker room The Lodge Poker Club was only a 13 min drive away. I could kill some time there no problem.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163462)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163463)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163464)

The place was really nice inside with plenty of tables and friendly staff. After getting my players account all set up  I waited for 20 min or so to get seated at a 1/2 500 max no limit Texas Holdem game.

The game was good and the players were friendly. I posted a breakdown of my favorite hand in the saloon here:

https://stacker.news/items/1602411/r/SatAttack?commentId=1602968

They had a table of treats for sale perhaps made staff member and I am sucker for both pastries and supporting small business so—win win. I got the pumpkin spice cake with cream cheese frosting (delicious). Here it is:

![](https://m.stacker.news/163465)

I only played for 1.5 hours and instead of going to the hotel to check in I headed straight to town to meet with @scoresby and @k00b which I was a bit nervous about. I’m not a very social person. But I was doubly excited to not only meet some real life bitcoiners, but fellow stackers! The pm stackers who created and build this place no less ! So off I went, nerves be damned. 

I found PlebLab easy enough. It’s a cool small space with ultimate hacker vibes. Scoresby and Koob came to say hey right away and were very cool and friendly. Koob wasn’t wearing any shoes, which is apparently normal for him, and as a fellow barefoot person, I give triple salute. Shoes suck. I’ve been a barefoot person my whole life and I too am barefoot at work every day. Kudos to Koob. He gave me some cool SN stickers and a cooler SN hat and pretty quickly Scoresby and I embarked on a city walk. I wish I would have thanked Koob for his founding and effort for curating this Bitcoin internet social for all of us but sadly I forgot.

It was very very cool talking to scoresby, what a guy. We had a lot of bitcoin related things to talk about which is so (pardon my French) fucking refreshing man. This is rare for me. Maybe for you too, dear reader. To be able to talk to a bitcoiner about bitcoin is so much fun. We can jump to this conclusion or that realization because we understand exactly where we are coming from in certain outlooks, opinions, knowledge, and world views. Scoresby is the man. He took me all around and showed me where there has been some awesome sounding Bitcoin events in the past. He showed me where the unchained head quarters is. He took me to Waller beach where walked along the Colorado River for a good ways. He showed me a bridge where apparently millions of bats live and come out at night in huge swarms. We could hear them chittering away. We saw a turtle. We saw a woman chatting on the phone in the grass with a HODL shirt on. Cool to see out in the wild, we both agreed.

He was quite curious about my poker playing and if someone is asking my about poker I have a hard time noticing anything else. So my recollection of surrounding details on the trail is a bit shoddy. I can rant and rant on that topic. I had a great time chatting it up and really appreciated his time taking me around. I loved talking and breathing bitcoin like it was a normal part of every day life. I felt submersed in its community just by chatting it up. We talked about the direction he would like SN to go and his efforts to make it happen. We spoke about current security incidents, cold storage options, SN sending wallet option past and present cultural shifts… it was great. Often I feel like I am the only real life bitcoiner out there when I’m surrounded by people who don’t know or don’t care but here in this moment, I felt the opposite. Perhaps it was the combination of being in a new city, talking to a new person, and seeing new things, but it felt like bitcoinization has already happened. It was normalized. We were the normal ones…

After an hour of walking we parted ways and it was time for me to EAT.

@plebpoet had suggested I go to a BBQ place called The Green Mesquite. “The real ones” go there she said. So not wanting to risk being a shoeby, that’s where I went.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163466)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163467)

Now the first thing I deeply appreciated was they had their own parking lot!! If you’ve ever been to Austin you know that parking here may be the only thing comparatively scarce to Bitcoin. The place has a real Texas saloon vibe to it and I thought just maybe this place has been here just as long as Austin. The man at the counter was friendly and had me sit anywhere. There was only one other person there. There were lots of old Texas decorations and Older country and blue grass songs playing which I appreciated. (Don’t like this new stuff in that genre)

I quickly decided that the best route would be a BBQ platter so I could try as many different things as possible. I went with the three meat choice and got smoked brisket, dark meat chicken, and sausage. My sides were green beans and fried okra and I got a shiner bock to wash it down with. Here it is:

![](https://m.stacker.news/163469)

Everything was delicious. I don’t know WHAT is going on with their BBQ sauce, sitting unceremoniously and unlabeled with all the other condiments, but it was amazing. It wasn’t crazy sweet and complimented the chicken and brisket so very well. I didn’t try on the sausage as I didn’t feel the need. It was so juicy and flavorful.

As I’m sitting finishing my beer something really wonderful happened. I saw a man through the window walking up, dirty and skinny and disheveled. He came through the door and I was too far to hear the words exchanged but I’m fairly certain he asked for a meal and said he couldn’t pay for it. Without anger or hesitation the guy working the counter said “I can do a sausage roll” and made him a small meal. The roll, some chips, and a water.

It was really wholesome and I can honestly say I’ve never seen anything like it.

I left shortly after and sat in my car and pulled up BTCmaps to see what sort of trouble I could get myself into. Just 7 min drive away there was a place listed called Local Pastures. Here is their BTCmap and website:

[https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:10791261306](https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:10791261306)

[https://www.localpastures.farm](https://www.localpastures.farm)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163470)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163471)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163472)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163473)

These guys are awesome! It’s a tiny little store the size of a large Kobe’s box and they get local meats, dairy’s, produce, and coffee and sell them here. When I walked in the first thing I noticed was their square terminal. They have the flip version. I poked around for maybe only a minute before asking the man if they accept bitcoin and he said “yep no problem.” Ha! Another victory for the books. Now it’s time to shop. Unfortunately the majority of their stuff required a kitchen to get use out of but the selection was quite nice. I had to settle for snacks. I got a couple of beef sticks and some pecans by two separate local farms.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163474)

When it was time to ring up he remembered I wanted to pay with sats and pretty quickly generated a lightning invoice before flipping it over to me. Easy day. Phoenix wallet again didn’t disappoint in speed and success. I asked him if he had ever heard of BTCmaps and he said no. I let him know that’s how I found this image and gave a brief explanation about what it is. He thought it was pretty cool when I showed him. I also asked if anyone else spends bitcoin there he said maybe once a month. He did say that for some stretch of time in the past there was a guy who would come 1-2 times a week and spend his sats there but he moved away. Perhaps that guy is a stacker. 

We had spoke a bit back at PlebLab about how disappointing BTCmaps can be. It definitely does not paint an accurate picture of where you can find places to spend your hard earned sats. So it felt good to get one first try. Maybe I’m lucky? Maybe I have a knack for finding the spots? Really I just liked that this one had a carrot as their symbol on the map and it was conveniently close by.

All in all, great day. I will now take a quick power nap and head back to the poker room for a couple hours of table time.

*Libertarian* here means adherence to the nonaggression principle as a legal framework and an Austrian style (zero tax) economy. I don't mean to refer to the political party that loosely associates with the name.

Defenders of tax/inflation based economies never seem to try to justify the moral position of their aggressive policies. They assert that governments provide the maximum possible utility through the process of taxing civilians and spending that money on "public" goods on their behalf. Democracy (also called socialism or communism), they say, is the arbiter that keeps the system in balance and removes corruption.

Libertarians (also called anarchocapitalists or voluntaryists) do not claim that aggression is acceptable, even if there was a democratic vote backing the aggression. They assert that there are both direct and indirect economic damages caused by taxation and inflation. The free market (also called capitalism), we say, is the arbiter that keeps the system in balance and removes corruption.

A question for anyone defending tax/inflation based economies with democratic governments: **Why are you paying for things you don't want?**

![](https://m.stacker.news/163586)

> US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh is a huge fan of the late economist Milton Friedman, the founding father of monetarism. And although targeting the money supply went out of fashion in the 1980s after its failure to control inflation adequately, Warsh is seeking to use his task forces to breathe new life into the idea.

> At his Jackson Hole speech in August, Warsh said: “We should pay attention to money created by the central bank and money that comes from the banking and financial systems. It’s true that financial innovations and other factors alter the mechanics that link the monetary base, the velocity of money and the broader economy. But that is scarcely a reason to ignore the ultimate effects of money on financial conditions and prices.”

Yes. *Monetary* policy without careful attention to *money* is retarded, at best.

## "Warsh has put two of his five task forces to work to bring monetarism back to the centre of Fed thinking."

Here's a nice summary of four decades of elite monetary thought:

> I am not going to delve into the long economic debate over the role of money in an economy, but will simply note that Friedman’s ideas became fashionable in the 1960s and 1970s following the failure of postwar Keynesian economics to control inflation. They were further boosted internationally by the Bundesbank’s remarkable success in achieving price stability in the 1970s using money supply as its primary indicator. But monetarism fell by the wayside a decade later when monetary indicators increasingly lost their ability to predict and target inflation.

> The waxing and waning of monetarism’s popularity was primarily a practical matter, although that did not stop huge doctrinal disputes in the profession and in politics.

> The main reason we are talking about monetarism again is practical. The money supply grew sharply during the post-Covid-19 pandemic period, especially in the US. Inflation followed soon after across the globe, as the chart below shows.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163587)

Yes, reality *sort of* vindicated monetarism quite a while back https://stacker.news/items/1565313

*Note:* The other option is to go some fiscal expectation route like [John Cochrane](https://x.com/joakimbook/status/2099845309140553967) does.

***

> It is obvious that excess money supply can generate inflation and the pandemic experience certainly tells us that ignoring money in an economy can be a serious oversight. At a minimum, Warsh is correct to call attention to the money supply. That is, after taking account of known reasons for monetary moves that are unlikely to affect prices, such as financial innovations and other developments that might affect the velocity of money. The point of that caveat is to remember that **if the speed that money flows around the economy slows — for example, if people cannot spend it in a pandemic — a larger stock will not necessarily be inflationary.**

I mean, yes -- for the time being. Like... *removing the safety pin of a grenade won't necessarily cause an explosion*. Just wait until dude lets go of the \[whatever-*that*-thing-is-called]. Or: *look, if I blow up a bubble nothing bad will necessarily happen...* yeah, until it pricks. Moron. 

> Interesting 2023 research from the Bank for International Settlements found that money supply movements generally do not matter if inflation is close to target. But during a highly inflationary episode, money’s importance grows strongly as a predictor of inflation. In short, **it would be very odd for monetary policymakers not to consider the potential effect of money on the price level and to think the interest rate is the sole thing that matters** for the transmission of policy to inflation.

OK, but now you're gaslighting us. Because a) *that was the case by economists and monetary policymakers for two decades*, and b) appealing to that belief was *exactly* why the transitory people got it so wrong in 2021-22!

*Jezus, fucks.*

> If there had been a sudden increase in money balances that spurred spending and inflation, you would expect a roughly uniform increase in the price level. But the European experience in 2022 was of an inflation overwhelmingly concentrated in energy and food prices. This suggests a supply shock, as European Central Bank chief economist Philip Lane has argued.

No it doesn't. Elasticities; many things at once. Also, (new) money has to go somewhere and if they went different places in different jurisdictions, **does that negate the monetary premise that excess money -> goods prices??**

Also, knock me over with a feather? There are lags; shadow banks/eurodollars matter too! (https://stacker.news/items/1595092)

items.title: Show Me the Incentive, and I'll Show You the Outcome - Obi
items.text:
This reads like a slop article, so don't bother reading the whole thing (below) unless you plan on skimming. But I think it's interesting for two reasons:

1. Obi takes a fairly open-minded approach to different custody solutions working for different people
2. His recommended best practices (while reasonable) are something I can't imagine any of my friends or family doing.

> different devices, different software, different supply chains, and failures that don't depend on each other. Then one compromised signer doesn't mean losing everything.

Seems to me like further evidence that bitcoin adoption comes when people are motivated enough to figure out how to do the above...and for most people in the world, that motivation doesn't exist yet.

--- 
The safest way to hold Bitcoin may not be the most profitable way to sell Bitcoin security.

Disclosure first: I ran a Bitcoin exchange, and it was profitable. Today I run a company with its own incentives. Read everything below with that in mind, because that is the point of the essay.

Charlie Munger said, "Show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome." Upton Sinclair put it more sharply: “It is difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on not understanding it.” Bitcoin custody advice is a case study in both. That isn't because people are dishonest. It's because incentives shape what we build, what we recommend, and eventually what everyone considers normal.

We have built an industry that talks endlessly about self-custody, decentralisation and removing trusted third parties. Yet many of its most prominent businesses make money by encouraging people to leave their Bitcoin with custodians, trade it more frequently, or buy proprietary devices to secure it. And much of the media explaining Bitcoin is funded by those same businesses.

## What an exchange is paid to do

An exchange makes money in three main ways: trading, listing more assets to trade, and higher-margin products like leverage, derivatives and lending. Increasingly, exchanges also earn from custody, subscriptions and other financial services, and customers who keep assets on the platform are easier to monetise than customers who withdraw. Most of these business models work best when your coins stay on the platform and keep moving.

I co-founded Coinfloor in 2013 and ran it until 2020. We explored all three revenue streams, including a derivatives subsidiary. But our spot exchange stayed almost entirely bitcoin-only. We focused on professional traders in the City, and our No-BS Bitcoin Guide told ordinary customers that if they weren't sure whether to trade, the answer was probably no.

We were profitable. My estimate is that we also left one to two orders of magnitude of potential revenue on the table by not pushing retail speculation, altcoins and leverage. I don't regret it. But it taught me that what is best for the customer and what is most profitable for the business are often different things.

Look at the industry's largest public company. In 2025 Coinbase earned about $4.06 billion from transactions, 59% of its net revenue, and bitcoin accounted for just 27% of its spot trading transaction revenue. Offering other assets isn't wrong in itself. But someone who buys bitcoin once, withdraws it and holds for a decade is worth very little to a trading business. Someone who keeps buying, selling, swapping and borrowing is worth a lot. A company can care about its customers and still be paid to encourage the behaviour that serves them least.

## The custody illusion

We describe moving coins to an exchange as reducing risk. It may reduce some risks, especially compared with careless self-custody. But it transfers and concentrates others. The exchange still has to protect the keys from hackers, insiders, social engineering and operational mistakes, and from AI-assisted attackers who get more capable every month. You haven't removed the custody problem. You've changed who carries it, and what shape it takes.

Choosing an exchange is a judgement that it will secure your bitcoin better than you would. That can be a sensible judgement. But we should state the trade-off honestly.

Professional custody doesn't eliminate risk. It pools it. Someone who compromises one person's wallet takes that person's money. Someone who compromises a major custodian can take funds belonging to many customers. In February 2025, the Bybit cold-wallet theft alone took $1.5 billion, the largest single theft in crypto history. A custodian can afford security teams, audits and controls that no individual can. But the reward for attacking it grows with the value it holds. Concentrating bitcoin concentrates the incentive to attack it.

Self-custody is not the safe alternative by default either. Chainalysis found that personal wallet compromises grew from 7.3% of stolen value in 2022 to 44% in 2024. In 2025 the share fell to roughly 20%, largely because the Bybit theft was so large. Excluding Bybit, it would have been roughly 37%. These are shares of reported thefts, not the odds of any individual being robbed. They don't tell us whether you're safer with a custodian or holding your own keys. They show that both approaches have serious failure modes.

## ETFs move the problem upstairs

ETFs give many investors a familiar, regulated way to get bitcoin exposure, and that has real value. But the bitcoin still has to be held somewhere, and much of it is held in one place. In its February 2026 shareholder letter, Coinbase said it custodies more than 80% of US Bitcoin and Ethereum ETF assets combined.

Institutional custody is a more serious operation than a retail exchange wallet, and some risks are better managed there. But an investor who sees shares in a brokerage account hasn't escaped custody risk. They own shares in a trust whose assets depend on a custodian's key management, legal arrangements and operational controls, several layers away from the coins. It may be well run. But when many funds share the same provider, infrastructure and security assumptions, a single weakness can hit all of them at once.

## The self-custody industry has incentives too

The standard answer is a hardware wallet. It is a genuine improvement over keeping keys on an internet-connected device. It is also a business that needs to sell devices, distinguish itself from competitors and sell upgrades.

In October 2026, the limits became visible. Ledger said a covert implant in devices sold through an authorised Southeast Asian reseller captured recovery phrases from the screen and transmitted them over a mobile network, and on-chain researchers estimated losses of up to $93 million. Ledger hasn't confirmed that total. By its account, its secure element and software were never compromised. They didn't need to be. The device's genuineness check reportedly passed because it authenticates the secure element, not whether every physical component is unmodified. The thing being verified wasn't the thing that failed.

Ledger said its own systems and direct sales channels were unaffected. The lesson is not that Ledger is uniquely vulnerable. It's that a security device can be compromised somewhere between manufacture and the moment its owner starts trusting it.

It won't be the last such incident. A dedicated device also does nothing against physical coercion, and a leaked customer list tells an attacker exactly whose door to knock on. Exchanges face the same problem with leaked customer data.

So the question isn't which device, provider or person to trust completely. As I argued in “[The Exploit Is Free](https://x.com/obi/status/2113284940871684209)”, it's how much you can lose when one of them fails.

## What no one is paid to recommend

The answer isn't a better single device. It's designing custody so that no single compromise can cost you everything: multisig across hardware and software from independent vendors, separated backups, and, where the setup supports them, time delays that slow down theft and spending limits that cap the damage.

Part of that can cost nothing. Most of us have an old laptop or phone in a drawer. With careful preparation, open-source signing software and the network permanently disabled, a general-purpose device can serve as an offline signer. You don't buy anything or wait for delivery, and no purchase record marks you as a bitcoin holder. A battered phone with a cracked screen attracts far less attention than a dedicated crypto device. An old laptop can even predate bitcoin, which makes it hard to believe it could contain malicious hardware designed to target bitcoin keys.

It isn't automatically secure. A general-purpose operating system has a larger attack surface, a second-hand device may already be compromised, and key generation and backups must be handled carefully. That's why I'd use it as one key in a multisig, alongside a hardware signer from another vendor and something like a  SeedSigner, rather than trusting it alone.

The exact design matters. Three different devices [aren't independent if they all rely on the same software](https://x.com/obi/status/2097700260910952790?s=20), the same setup process or the same backup. A badly implemented multisig can introduce new problems, and a commercial hardware wallet may be the safer starting point for someone without the expertise to prepare a DIY signer. But the principle holds: different devices, different software, different supply chains, and failures that don't depend on each other. Then one compromised signer doesn't mean losing everything.

So why does almost nobody suggest this? Partly because commercial devices are easier to use, document and support. But also because no company earns anything by persuading you to reuse the phone in your drawer.

There's no affiliate link for the phone you already own. No device sale, no upgrade cycle, no marketing budget.

There's a deeper problem too. The industry isn't just rewarded for selling particular products. It has little reason to promote setups designed so that no single product matters very much. Yet that is exactly what good security architecture does.

## Who pays the people we listen to

Bitcoin podcasts, educators and conferences need funding, and nobody should be expected to work for free. But the sponsors who can pay are the businesses that profit from acquiring customers. An exchange knows what a new trader is worth. A hardware maker knows what a device sale is worth. An open-source project encouraging DIY multisig can't compete with either.

So audiences hear the same recommendations again and again. Repetition becomes familiarity, familiarity becomes credibility, and credibility becomes conventional wisdom. That doesn't require a conspiracy or anyone being consciously dishonest. Many hosts genuinely believe in the products they promote, and many of those products deserve it. That's exactly what makes incentives powerful: they shape beliefs without anyone deciding to mislead.

## My incentives

I definitely have incentives. I actively support Fedimint and run Fedi, which is a business, not a charity. A federation is custody too, with its own trust assumptions and its own ways to fail. It would be hypocritical to examine everyone else's incentives and exempt my own, so hold me to the same standard.

Judge us by what we've done. Fedimint creator Eric Sirion and I became involved in Fedimint because we believed Bitcoin needed ways to scale that preserve privacy and spread custody across communities. We've also supported BitVM, followed Ark and Pipes with interest, and I'm excited about federated Cashu. Some of these will compete with us. Good. If one company or protocol ended up owning bitcoin custody, I would consider that a failure, even if it were us.

Daniel Krawisz put it as being a speculative philanthropist rather than a venture capitalist. Build what Bitcoin needs, find sustainable ways to pay for it, and don't mistake your company's success for Bitcoin's. The test is whether we back better solutions when someone else captures the value. If many independent companies succeed and Fedi doesn't, but Bitcoin becomes more private, scalable and secure, I would still consider that a good outcome. A world where everyone's bitcoin depends on three custodians and one device supply chain would not be.

## Follow the incentives. Then change them.

The solution isn't to boycott exchanges, hardware wallets or sponsored media. All three provide real value. It's to recognise that the most heavily promoted answer isn't always the best one, and then to change what gets rewarded. That means funding open-source security tools that have no business model, disclosing sponsorships clearly, and comparing custody approaches honestly.

Judge security by what happens when something goes wrong. When a signer is compromised, a provider disappears or a vulnerability is found, does the damage stay contained? Can people recover? Does one company's failure become everybody's failure? As AI makes finding exploits cheaper, those are the questions that matter.

The right setup might include a commercial hardware wallet, a reused phone, several independent devices, multiple people, or a federation of professional operators. It depends on what you're protecting, from whom, and what you can realistically operate safely. But it should be chosen for the security of the system, not for who earns a commission when you adopt it.

Bitcoin was created to change the incentives of money. If we want better outcomes from the industry built around it, we need better incentives there too.

Rarely persuaded by moonboi shit like this.... but *today might be the day!*

Is the thing working? Are we running off to the moon? No, we're stuck in the same god-awful trench we've been in for over a year and arguably for about 5 years. *Where is this orange dream of which you speak?*

We got everything right -- and world events keep validating that -- but the market says no. That's very discouraging. (And usually, a sign that you're wrong.)

> the case for non-sovereign, censorship-resistant, hard money should not be forgotten because it will not go away.

***

I don't love this kind of cope and chart porn but it *is* a pretty chart:

***

Alex's case is four-fold: **TECHNICAL**, **POSITIONING**, **FUNDAMENTAL**, and **SENTIMENT**

## Technical: the 50W MA has shifted into upward trajectory

Fifth week in a row of closing above... *we're going to the moon*.

There's a long-term, long-standing pattern (as if events from a decade ago are informative to this novel asset today):

> How often has a reclaim been followed by a new leg down? Of the 13 completed reclaims since 2011, the split is how long the price had been below the average. The four that ended spells of 20 weeks or more 1) never closed more than 8.4% below the reclaim level in the following year; 2) were +1497%, +128%, +55%, +142% higher a year later; and 3) regained the prior all-time high within 33–83 weeks. Of the nine that ended spells of 14 weeks or less, seven fell more than 25% within a year. September's reclaim ended a 44-week spell (Chart 2). This is a pattern.

> The four-year cycle agrees. The three completed cycles printed their lows on days 777, 889 and 912 after their halvings; this cycle's low so far came on day 802, and yesterday was day 916.

It's time. Even Saylor's AI-slopped bull says so. https://stacker.news/items/1600946

Here's another aspect that annoys the fucking out of me: the double-standings/goal-shifting.

> This was the shallowest bear on record (-53% against -93%, -85%, -84%, -77% before it) and the first in which price never traded below the network’s cost basis: the ratio of market value to realized value bottomed at 1.10, against 0.56, 0.69 and 0.75 at the three prior lows.

We can spin "this was the shallowest bear" into *makes sense* by saying a) institutions are here, big-money bids etc, b) we're growing up so bears will be shallower. It's empty. Nobody (in high finance) is here.

Reporting institutions held 355k BTC-equivalent of the spot ETFs at the Sept. 30, 2025, quarter-end, the last before the high, and 307k by June 2026 (-14%), and the decline sits almost entirely with the multi-strategy and macro funds, basis desks, and bank trading books that used the ETFs for carry and momentum

> The S\&P 500 is 0.8% below a record set on Oct. 6 and the Nasdaq 100 4.5% below its own, while gold is 22% below January's high. Bitcoin, at Thursday’s price, is 35% below its high, so a 53% rise only returns it to a price it traded at a year ago (Chart 11). **The alternative to all of them is cash.** A bet against stocks and hard assets is a bet in favor of fiat, the one asset its issuer has promised, through $2 trillion deficits and a 5% 10-year Treasury, to keep diluting.
